definition: In computational linguistics the Yarowsky algorithm is an unsupervised learning algorithm for word sense disambiguation that uses the "one sense per collocation" and the "one sense per discourse" properties of human languages for word sense disambiguation.
details: From observation, words tend to exhibit only one sense in most given discourse and in a given collocation.

explainer.lead: The Yarowsky algorithm is an unsupervised method for word sense disambiguation that relies on how senses behave across collocations and discourse. It matters because it needs no sense-labelled training data, using unlabelled text and a few seed examples instead.

tiers.eli5: If a word is used one way in a sentence, it is probably used the same way throughout that passage, so you can guess its meaning from a few clear examples and spread the answer.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers seed a few labelled examples per sense, then iteratively label more occurrences and retrain, exploiting one-sense-per-collocation and one-sense-per-discourse. A common pitfall is that early mistakes get reinforced across iterations, so seed quality matters greatly.
tiers.paperLevel: The algorithm uses the one-sense-per-collocation and one-sense-per-discourse properties of language and bootstraps from a small seed set; it can propagate errors and its guarantees depend on those properties holding.

explainer.example: Given a few seed uses of a word in one sense, the algorithm labels matching collocations, then labels other occurrences in the same documents, iterating until labels stabilise.
